Get ready to take control of your network's traffic engineering!

screens.title: Why BGP Path Control Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Effective BGP path control is absolutely paramount for anyone managing a multi-homed network today. While BGP's best path selection algorithm provides a robust default process for choosing routes, it often doesn't align perfectly with specific business or technical requirements. Imagine you need to prioritize a certain ISP link for cost reasons, or ensure critical traffic uses a high-bandwidth connection, or even steer traffic away from a congested path. This is where BGP path control mechanisms become indispensable. They allow network engineers to strategically override BGP's default decisions. In this chapter, we'll focus on three primary attributes: Local Preference, Multi-Exit Discriminator, and AS-Path Prepending. Each offers a unique way to influence BGP's path selection, and understanding their nuances is a critical skill. These mechanisms are not just about making traffic go 'somewhere'; they're about making it go the 'right way' – optimizing performance, ensuring high availability, and managing operational costs. Without these tools, your network would be at the mercy of default routing decisions, which might not always serve your organization's best interests. So, let's dive into how we can take control.

screens.title: Local Preference: Influencing Outbound Traffic
screens.narratorSegment: Let's begin our deep dive with Local Preference, a fundamental BGP attribute. Local Preference is a well-known discretionary attribute, meaning it's always present in BGP updates, but its value can be changed. Crucially, it's exchanged *only* among IBGP peers within the same autonomous system. This is a key distinction: it never leaves your AS. Its primary function is to influence outbound traffic from your AS. When a router within your AS needs to send traffic to an external destination, it will always prefer the path that has the highest Local Preference value. Think of it as an internal 'exit preference' score. By assigning a higher Local Preference to routes learned via a specific external link, you can effectively steer all internal traffic towards that preferred exit point, perhaps a primary ISP link or a link with better performance. The default Local Preference value is 100. For example, if you have two connections to the internet, one to ISP-A and another to ISP-B, and you want all outbound traffic to prefer ISP-A, you would configure an import policy on the router peering with ISP-A to set a higher Local Preference, say 200, for all routes received from ISP-A. This ensures your internal routers consistently choose ISP-A for external destinations. Understanding this internal scope is vital to avoid common misconfigurations.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Local Preference: Outbound Traffic
BGP Attribute Deep Dive

Local Preference: Influencing Outbound Traffic

An IBGP Attribute for Internal Path Selection

IBGP Only

Exchanged only among IBGP peers within the same Autonomous System (AS).

Outbound Traffic

Primary function is to influence how your AS sends traffic to external destinations.

Higher is Preferred

Routers prefer paths with a higher Local Preference value.

Key Takeaway

Local Preference is an IBGP attribute used to steer outbound traffic from an AS, with higher values indicating a more preferred exit path.

Local Preference in Action
Traffic prefers the path with the highest Local Preference value.

screens.title: Configuring Local Preference in Junos OS
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's translate the concept of Local Preference into a practical Junos OS configuration. We'll use a scenario where your AS has two internet connections, one to ISP-A and another to ISP-B. Our goal is to make ISP-A the primary path for most outbound traffic, but with an exception: specific prefixes should always use ISP-B. First, we define a prefix-list for those specific routes, like 192.0.2.0 slash 24. Then, we create a policy called SET underscore LP underscore ISP underscore A. This policy, applied as an import policy on the router peering with ISP-A, sets a Local Preference of 200 for all routes received from ISP-A, making them generally preferred. Next, for ISP-B, we create SET underscore LP underscore ISP underscore B. This policy has two terms. The first term matches our specific prefixes and assigns an even higher Local Preference, say 250, ensuring they *always* go via ISP-B. The second term sets a lower Local Preference, like 150, for all other routes from ISP-B, making them less preferred than ISP-A's general routes. These policies are then applied to the respective BGP groups or neighbors. This granular control allows you to precisely engineer your outbound traffic, ensuring that your network's exit points are utilized according to your specific operational and cost-efficiency goals. Remember, Local Preference is a powerful tool for internal traffic steering.

keyIdea.title: Junos LP Configuration
keyIdea.text: Junos OS uses import policies with the `local-preference <value>` action to configure Local Preference, directing outbound traffic.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Configuring Local Preference
Junos OS Configuration

Configuring Local Preference in Junos OS

Policy-Based Outbound Traffic Steering

[edit policy-options]
prefix-list PREFER_ISP_B_FOR_THESE {
    192.0.2.0/24;
}

policy-statement SET_LP_ISP_A {
    term ALL_ROUTES_ISP_A {
        from protocol bgp;
        then {
            local-preference 200; # Prefer ISP-A generally
            accept;
        }
    }
}

policy-statement SET_LP_ISP_B {
    term SPECIFIC_ROUTES_ISP_B {
        from {
            protocol bgp;
            prefix-list PREFER_ISP_B_FOR_THESE;
        }
        then {
            local-preference 250; # Even higher LP for specific prefixes via ISP-B
            accept;
        }
    }
    term ALL_OTHER_ROUTES_ISP_B {
        from protocol bgp;
        then {
            local-preference 150; # Lower LP for other routes via ISP-B
            accept;
        }
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Junos OS uses import policies with the `local-preference <value>` action to configure Local Preference, directing outbound traffic.

Prefix-List Definition

Identifies specific routes that require special handling, allowing granular control.

Policy for ISP-A

Sets a higher Local Preference (e.g., 200) for all routes received from ISP-A, making it the general preferred outbound path.

Policy for ISP-B

Uses multiple terms to set an even higher Local Preference for specific prefixes, and a lower one for general routes, via ISP-B.

Pro-Tip

Apply these policies as import policies to the respective BGP groups or neighbors to ensure they take effect on incoming routes.

screens.title: Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED): Influencing Inbound Traffic
screens.narratorSegment: Moving on to our second path control mechanism, the Multi-Exit Discriminator, or MED. Unlike Local Preference, MED is an optional non-transitive attribute, meaning it's not always present and it doesn't typically pass beyond the immediate neighboring AS. Its purpose is to influence inbound traffic into your autonomous system when there are multiple entry points from a *single* neighboring AS. Here's the crucial point: a lower MED value indicates a more preferred path. So, if you want an external AS to send traffic to you via a specific link, you'd advertise your routes with a lower MED on that link. The key limitation of MED, and a common source of confusion, is that it is *only* compared between routes received from the *same* neighboring AS. This means if you have two different ISPs, MED values from ISP A will not be compared with MED values from ISP B. MED is typically used when you have redundant links to the *same* ISP and want to guide that ISP on which link to use to send traffic to you. The default MED value is 0. For instance, if you have two links to ISP-A and want ISP-A to prefer sending traffic to you via 'link-1' for general traffic, you would advertise your prefixes with a lower MED on 'link-1' compared to 'link-2'. This allows you to subtly guide your direct neighbor's routing decisions.

Module 3›Chapter 3.3›MED: Inbound Traffic
BGP Attribute Deep Dive

Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED): Influencing Inbound Traffic

An EBGP Attribute for Neighboring AS Path Selection

EBGP Attribute

Optional non-transitive attribute, typically not passed beyond the immediate neighbor.

Inbound Traffic

Influences how a neighboring AS sends traffic into your AS.

Lower is Preferred

A lower MED value indicates a more preferred path for inbound traffic.

Key Takeaway

MED is an optional non-transitive EBGP attribute that influences inbound traffic from a *single* neighboring AS; lower values are preferred.

MED in Action (Same ISP)
ISP-A prefers the path with the lower MED value to reach your AS.

screens.title: Configuring MED in Junos OS
screens.narratorSegment: Let's now look at how to implement MED in Junos OS. Consider a scenario where your AS has two links to ISP-A, and you want ISP-A to prefer sending traffic to your AS via link-1 for general traffic, but via link-2 for a specific service hosted on 10.0.0.0 slash 24. We start by defining a prefix-list for our SERVICE underscore PREFIX, which is 10.0.0.0 slash 24. Then, we create an export policy, SET underscore MED underscore TO underscore ISP underscore A underscore LINK1. This policy will be applied to the BGP group or neighbor associated with link-1. Within this policy, the first term matches our SERVICE underscore PREFIX and sets a lower MED, for example, metric 10. This tells ISP-A to prefer link-1 for this specific service traffic. The second term, ALL underscore OTHER underscore TRAFFIC, sets a higher MED, such as metric 50, for all other routes advertised via link-1. This makes link-1 less preferred for general traffic compared to link-2 (assuming link-2 has a policy with lower MEDs for general traffic). This policy is applied as an export policy, meaning it influences what your router advertises to ISP-A. Remember, the 'metric' action in Junos OS is used to set the MED attribute. This precise control allows you to guide your direct neighbor's inbound routing decisions, optimizing traffic flow for specific services or general connectivity.

keyIdea.title: Junos MED Configuration
keyIdea.text: Junos OS uses export policies with the `metric <value>` action to configure MED, influencing inbound traffic from a specific neighboring AS.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Configuring MED
Junos OS Configuration

Configuring MED in Junos OS

Policy-Based Inbound Traffic Steering from a Neighboring AS

[edit policy-options]
prefix-list SERVICE_PREFIX {
    10.0.0.0/24;
}

policy-statement SET_MED_TO_ISP_A_LINK1 {
    term SERVICE_TRAFFIC {
        from {
            protocol bgp;
            prefix-list SERVICE_PREFIX;
        }
        then {
            metric 10; # Lower MED for service traffic via link-1
            accept;
        }
    }
    term ALL_OTHER_TRAFFIC {
        from protocol bgp;
        then {
            metric 50; # Higher MED for other traffic via link-1
            accept;
        }
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Junos OS uses export policies with the `metric <value>` action to configure MED, influencing inbound traffic from a specific neighboring AS.

Prefix-List for Services

Defines specific service prefixes that require distinct MED values for traffic steering.

Policy for Link-1

Sets a lower MED for service traffic and a higher MED for general traffic advertised via Link-1.

Common Mistake

Forgetting that MED is only compared between routes received from the *same* neighboring AS. It cannot influence traffic from different ISPs.

screens.title: AS-Path Prepending: Influencing Inbound Traffic from Any AS
screens.narratorSegment: Our final BGP path control mechanism is AS-Path Prepending, a powerful technique used to influence inbound traffic into your AS from *any* external AS. This method works by making your AS appear 'further away' for certain routes. How does it achieve this? By prepending your own AS number, or any other AS number, multiple times to the AS_Path attribute when you advertise your routes. The standard practice is to prepend your own AS number. Since a shorter AS_Path is generally preferred in the BGP best path selection algorithm, prepending effectively makes the path less attractive to external networks. This is particularly useful when you have multiple ISPs and want to make one ISP less preferred for inbound traffic compared to another, or when you want to designate a specific link as a backup. For example, if you have two ISPs, ISP-A and ISP-B, and you want ISP-A to be the primary for inbound traffic for your entire AS, you would prepend your AS number multiple times when advertising your prefixes to ISP-B. This makes the path through ISP-B seem longer and less desirable to the rest of the internet, ensuring that most inbound traffic flows through ISP-A. It's a simple yet highly effective way to globally influence how others perceive the 'distance' to your network.

BGP Attribute Deep Dive

AS-Path Prepending: Influencing Inbound Traffic from Any AS

Lengthening the AS_Path for Path De-prioritization

Lengthen AS_Path

Adds your own AS number multiple times to the AS_Path attribute.

Shorter Path Preferred

Makes the path appear longer and thus less attractive in BGP best path selection.

Influences Any AS

Affects how *any* external AS sends traffic into your autonomous system.

Key Takeaway

AS-Path Prepending lengthens the AS_Path attribute, making a route less attractive to *any* external AS, thus influencing inbound traffic.

AS-Path Prepending in Action
External ASes prefer the shorter AS_Path via ISP-A.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's now configure AS-Path Prepending in Junos OS. Imagine you have two ISPs, ISP-A and ISP-B. Your goal is to make ISP-A the primary path for inbound traffic to your AS, and ISP-B the backup. To achieve this, you need to make the routes advertised to ISP-B appear less attractive to the rest of the internet. We'll create an export policy called PREPEND underscore TO underscore ISP underscore B. This policy will be applied to the BGP group or neighbor connected to ISP-B. Within this policy, we use the as-path prepend action. For instance, as-path prepend "65000 65000 65000" will add your AS number, let's say 65000, three times to the AS_Path attribute. This effectively lengthens the path for any routes advertised to ISP-B. When other ASes receive these routes, the longer AS_Path through ISP-B will be less preferred compared to the shorter AS_Path through ISP-A, which does not have prepending. This ensures that most inbound traffic will naturally gravitate towards ISP-A. It's crucial to apply this as an export policy, as you are influencing what your AS advertises to its neighbors. This technique provides a global influence on inbound traffic, making it a versatile tool for traffic engineering across different external connections.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Configuring AS-Path Prepending
Junos OS Configuration

Configuring AS-Path Prepending in Junos OS

Policy-Based Inbound Traffic De-prioritization

[edit policy-options]
policy-statement PREPEND_TO_ISP_B {
    term PREPEND_AS {
        from protocol bgp; # Or specific prefixes you want to prepend
        then {
            as-path prepend "65000 65000 65000"; # Prepend your AS (e.g., 65000) three times
            accept;
        }
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Junos OS uses export policies with the `as-path prepend <AS-number>` action to lengthen the AS_Path, de-prioritizing inbound traffic.

Export Policy Creation

Define a policy that will be applied to routes advertised to the less preferred ISP.

`as-path prepend` Action

Use this action to add your AS number multiple times, making the path appear longer.

Pro-Tip

Typically, 2-4 prepends are sufficient. Excessive prepending can make your routes appear too far away and potentially cause them to be filtered.

screens.title: Avoiding Common BGP Path Control Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: As powerful as these BGP path control mechanisms are, they also come with common pitfalls that can lead to unexpected routing behavior if not handled carefully. Let's review some crucial safety notes. For Local Preference, a frequent mistake is applying it incorrectly, perhaps thinking it influences inbound traffic, when its scope is strictly for *outbound* traffic within your AS. Always remember it's an IBGP attribute. For the Multi-Exit Discriminator, the biggest pitfall is forgetting its limited scope: MED is *only* compared between routes received from the *same* neighboring AS. Trying to use MED to influence traffic from different ISPs simply won't work, as the values are not compared across different ASes. Finally, with AS-Path Prepending, ensure you prepend your *own* AS number or an AS number that is logically consistent with your peering agreements. Prepending arbitrary or excessive AS numbers can make your routes unreachable or undesirable to other networks. While technically possible to prepend other AS numbers, it's generally not recommended for stability. Always verify the AS_Path using commands like show route protocol bgp detail or show bgp neighbor advertised-routes to confirm your prepending is working as expected. As with all BGP policies, changes can have a significant impact on network connectivity, so always test thoroughly in a lab environment before deploying to production. Precision and verification are your best allies here.

screens.title: Comparing BGP Path Control Mechanisms
screens.narratorSegment: To bring everything together, let's quickly compare Local Preference, MED, and AS-Path Prepending. Understanding their distinct characteristics is key to choosing the right tool for your traffic engineering needs. Local Preference is your go-to for influencing outbound traffic from your autonomous system. It's an internal IBGP attribute, meaning its influence is confined within your AS, and higher values are always preferred. You'd use it to steer your internal routers towards a specific exit point. In Junos, you configure it with local-preference in an import policy. MED, or Multi-Exit Discriminator, is designed to influence inbound traffic into your AS, but with a critical limitation: it only works when you have multiple entry points from the *same* neighboring AS. It's an EBGP attribute, and lower values are preferred. You'd use it to guide a specific ISP on which link to use to send traffic to you. In Junos, you set it with metric in an export policy. Finally, AS-Path Prepending is your most powerful tool for influencing inbound traffic from *any* external AS. It works by lengthening the AS_Path attribute, making your routes appear less desirable to the broader internet. You'd use it to make a particular ISP a backup for inbound traffic. In Junos, you configure it with as-path prepend in an export policy. By strategically applying these attributes, you can precisely engineer traffic flows to meet your network's performance, resilience, and cost objectives. Each mechanism has its unique role, and mastering them provides unparalleled control over your network's external connectivity.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to this crucial chapter on BGP Path Control Mechanisms. In today's interconnected world, simply having multiple internet connections isn't enough; you need precise control over how traffic enters and leaves your network. This chapter will equip you with the knowledge to master three fundamental BGP attributes: Local Preference, Multi-Exit Discriminator, and AS-Path Prepending. These tools are essential for any network engineer looking to optimize traffic flow, enhance network availability, and effectively manage operational costs in multi-homed environments. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how to strategically influence BGP's best path selection process, moving beyond default behaviors to meet specific business and technical requirements. We'll explore each mechanism in detail, including practical Junos OS configurations, so you can confidently apply these concepts in real-world scenarios. Get ready to take control of your network's traffic engineering!

In this first part of our learning objectives, we'll lay the groundwork for understanding how to influence traffic flow using BGP. Our primary goal is to empower you to explain the critical role of Local Preference in dictating how your autonomous system sends traffic out to the internet. You'll learn not just what Local Preference is, but also how to configure Junos OS policies to precisely set and manipulate this attribute, ensuring your outbound traffic takes the most optimal or cost-effective path. Following that, we'll shift our focus to the Multi-Exit Discriminator, or MED. You'll be able to describe exactly how MED influences inbound traffic, specifically from a single neighboring autonomous system, allowing you to guide external networks on how to reach you. This foundational knowledge is key to building resilient and efficient multi-homed networks.

Continuing our journey through BGP path control, our next set of objectives will delve into more advanced techniques for influencing inbound traffic. You will gain a comprehensive understanding of AS-Path Prepending, learning its purpose and how it's applied to make your network appear 'further away' for certain routes, thereby influencing how any external AS sends traffic to you. This is a powerful tool for traffic engineering, especially when dealing with multiple distinct ISPs. Crucially, you'll also learn how to implement Junos OS policies to set and modify the MED attribute, giving you hands-on skills to direct inbound traffic from a specific neighbor. Finally, we'll cover the practical configuration of Junos OS policies to prepend AS numbers to the AS_Path attribute, solidifying your ability to apply these concepts in a real-world Juniper environment. These skills are invaluable for fine-tuning your network's external connectivity.

Effective BGP path control is absolutely paramount for anyone managing a multi-homed network today. While BGP's best path selection algorithm provides a robust default process for choosing routes, it often doesn't align perfectly with specific business or technical requirements. Imagine you need to prioritize a certain ISP link for cost reasons, or ensure critical traffic uses a high-bandwidth connection, or even steer traffic away from a congested path. This is where BGP path control mechanisms become indispensable. They allow network engineers to strategically override BGP's default decisions. In this chapter, we'll focus on three primary attributes: Local Preference, Multi-Exit Discriminator, and AS-Path Prepending. Each offers a unique way to influence BGP's path selection, and understanding their nuances is a critical skill. These mechanisms are not just about making traffic go 'somewhere'; they're about making it go the 'right way' – optimizing performance, ensuring high availability, and managing operational costs. Without these tools, your network would be at the mercy of default routing decisions, which might not always serve your organization's best interests. So, let's dive into how we can take control.

Let's begin our deep dive with Local Preference, a fundamental BGP attribute. Local Preference is a well-known discretionary attribute, meaning it's always present in BGP updates, but its value can be changed. Crucially, it's exchanged *only* among IBGP peers within the same autonomous system. This is a key distinction: it never leaves your AS. Its primary function is to influence outbound traffic from your AS. When a router within your AS needs to send traffic to an external destination, it will always prefer the path that has the highest Local Preference value. Think of it as an internal 'exit preference' score. By assigning a higher Local Preference to routes learned via a specific external link, you can effectively steer all internal traffic towards that preferred exit point, perhaps a primary ISP link or a link with better performance. The default Local Preference value is 100. For example, if you have two connections to the internet, one to ISP-A and another to ISP-B, and you want all outbound traffic to prefer ISP-A, you would configure an import policy on the router peering with ISP-A to set a higher Local Preference, say 200, for all routes received from ISP-A. This ensures your internal routers consistently choose ISP-A for external destinations. Understanding this internal scope is vital to avoid common misconfigurations.

Now, let's translate the concept of Local Preference into a practical Junos OS configuration. We'll use a scenario where your AS has two internet connections, one to ISP-A and another to ISP-B. Our goal is to make ISP-A the primary path for most outbound traffic, but with an exception: specific prefixes should always use ISP-B. First, we define a prefix-list for those specific routes, like 192.0.2.0 slash 24. Then, we create a policy called SET underscore LP underscore ISP underscore A. This policy, applied as an import policy on the router peering with ISP-A, sets a Local Preference of 200 for all routes received from ISP-A, making them generally preferred. Next, for ISP-B, we create SET underscore LP underscore ISP underscore B. This policy has two terms. The first term matches our specific prefixes and assigns an even higher Local Preference, say 250, ensuring they *always* go via ISP-B. The second term sets a lower Local Preference, like 150, for all other routes from ISP-B, making them less preferred than ISP-A's general routes. These policies are then applied to the respective BGP groups or neighbors. This granular control allows you to precisely engineer your outbound traffic, ensuring that your network's exit points are utilized according to your specific operational and cost-efficiency goals. Remember, Local Preference is a powerful tool for internal traffic steering.

Moving on to our second path control mechanism, the Multi-Exit Discriminator, or MED. Unlike Local Preference, MED is an optional non-transitive attribute, meaning it's not always present and it doesn't typically pass beyond the immediate neighboring AS. Its purpose is to influence inbound traffic into your autonomous system when there are multiple entry points from a *single* neighboring AS. Here's the crucial point: a lower MED value indicates a more preferred path. So, if you want an external AS to send traffic to you via a specific link, you'd advertise your routes with a lower MED on that link. The key limitation of MED, and a common source of confusion, is that it is *only* compared between routes received from the *same* neighboring AS. This means if you have two different ISPs, MED values from ISP A will not be compared with MED values from ISP B. MED is typically used when you have redundant links to the *same* ISP and want to guide that ISP on which link to use to send traffic to you. The default MED value is 0. For instance, if you have two links to ISP-A and want ISP-A to prefer sending traffic to you via 'link-1' for general traffic, you would advertise your prefixes with a lower MED on 'link-1' compared to 'link-2'. This allows you to subtly guide your direct neighbor's routing decisions.

Let's now look at how to implement MED in Junos OS. Consider a scenario where your AS has two links to ISP-A, and you want ISP-A to prefer sending traffic to your AS via link-1 for general traffic, but via link-2 for a specific service hosted on 10.0.0.0 slash 24. We start by defining a prefix-list for our SERVICE underscore PREFIX, which is 10.0.0.0 slash 24. Then, we create an export policy, SET underscore MED underscore TO underscore ISP underscore A underscore LINK1. This policy will be applied to the BGP group or neighbor associated with link-1. Within this policy, the first term matches our SERVICE underscore PREFIX and sets a lower MED, for example, metric 10. This tells ISP-A to prefer link-1 for this specific service traffic. The second term, ALL underscore OTHER underscore TRAFFIC, sets a higher MED, such as metric 50, for all other routes advertised via link-1. This makes link-1 less preferred for general traffic compared to link-2 (assuming link-2 has a policy with lower MEDs for general traffic). This policy is applied as an export policy, meaning it influences what your router advertises to ISP-A. Remember, the 'metric' action in Junos OS is used to set the MED attribute. This precise control allows you to guide your direct neighbor's inbound routing decisions, optimizing traffic flow for specific services or general connectivity.

Our final BGP path control mechanism is AS-Path Prepending, a powerful technique used to influence inbound traffic into your AS from *any* external AS. This method works by making your AS appear 'further away' for certain routes. How does it achieve this? By prepending your own AS number, or any other AS number, multiple times to the AS_Path attribute when you advertise your routes. The standard practice is to prepend your own AS number. Since a shorter AS_Path is generally preferred in the BGP best path selection algorithm, prepending effectively makes the path less attractive to external networks. This is particularly useful when you have multiple ISPs and want to make one ISP less preferred for inbound traffic compared to another, or when you want to designate a specific link as a backup. For example, if you have two ISPs, ISP-A and ISP-B, and you want ISP-A to be the primary for inbound traffic for your entire AS, you would prepend your AS number multiple times when advertising your prefixes to ISP-B. This makes the path through ISP-B seem longer and less desirable to the rest of the internet, ensuring that most inbound traffic flows through ISP-A. It's a simple yet highly effective way to globally influence how others perceive the 'distance' to your network.

Let's now configure AS-Path Prepending in Junos OS. Imagine you have two ISPs, ISP-A and ISP-B. Your goal is to make ISP-A the primary path for inbound traffic to your AS, and ISP-B the backup. To achieve this, you need to make the routes advertised to ISP-B appear less attractive to the rest of the internet. This effectively lengthens the path for any routes advertised to ISP-B. This ensures that most inbound traffic will naturally gravitate towards ISP-A. It's crucial to apply this as an export policy, as you are influencing what your AS advertises to its neighbors. This technique provides a global influence on inbound traffic, making it a versatile tool for traffic engineering across different external connections.

As powerful as these BGP path control mechanisms are, they also come with common pitfalls that can lead to unexpected routing behavior if not handled carefully. Let's review some crucial safety notes. While technically possible to prepend other AS numbers, it's generally not recommended for stability. Always verify the AS_Path using commands like show route protocol bgp detail or show bgp neighbor advertised-routes to confirm your prepending is working as expected. As with all BGP policies, changes can have a significant impact on network connectivity, so always test thoroughly in a lab environment before deploying to production. Precision and verification are your best allies here.
